stimulus.title: Exercício C1: ciências naturais (meta de 6 min)
stimulus.content:
PASSAGE: Bioluminescence in Marine Organisms

Bioluminescence, the production of light by a living organism, is remarkably common in the ocean, appearing in bacteria, jellyfish, fish, and even some sharks. Unlike an incandescent bulb, which wastes most of its energy as heat, bioluminescent light comes from a highly efficient chemical reaction between a molecule called luciferin and an enzyme called luciferase. Because so little energy is lost as heat, biologists sometimes call it "cold light."

Organisms use this light in several ways. Some use it defensively: certain squid release a glowing cloud instead of ink, startling predators long enough to escape. Others use it to hunt. The anglerfish, perhaps the most famous example, dangles a glowing lure above its mouth to attract prey close enough to seize. Still others use light to communicate. In the deep sea, darkness is nearly absolute, so visual signals cannot rely on ambient light at all, and even in shallow water at night, tiny crustaceans called ostracods produce synchronized displays to attract mates.

What especially interests evolutionary biologists is that bioluminescence did not evolve just once. Genetic and biochemical evidence shows that it has arisen independently dozens of times in unrelated lineages, often through different chemical pathways. This pattern, in which unrelated organisms evolve similar traits independently, is known as convergent evolution, and bioluminescence is one of its most striking examples.

prompt: Ideia principal. What is the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Bioluminescence is a rare adaptation found only in a few deep-sea species.
options.B: Bioluminescence is a widespread, chemically efficient trait that serves multiple functions and evolved independently many times.
options.C: The anglerfish, which uses a glowing lure to catch its prey, is the most important example of bioluminescence.
options.D: Bioluminescent light is less efficient than artificial light because much of its energy is lost as heat.

explanation: Cobre os três eixos (o que é + eficiência, funções, evolução independente). (A) contradiz "remarkably common"; (C) é detalhe, e o texto diz "perhaps the most famous", não "o mais importante"; (D) inverte a comparação com a lâmpada.

stimulus.title: Exercício C2: história (meta de 6 min)
stimulus.content:
PASSAGE: Coffee Houses in Seventeenth-Century England

The first English coffee house opened in Oxford in 1650; within two decades, London alone had hundreds. For the price of a single cup, a customer could sit for hours, read the newspapers provided by the house, and join whatever conversation was underway. Because admission was cheap and open to any man who could pay, merchants, scholars, clergymen, and minor gentry sat at the same long tables.

This mixing had consequences well beyond casual talk. Particular houses became known for particular subjects: men interested in maritime insurance gathered at Lloyd's, while those following scientific debates went to the houses near the Royal Society. Information that had once circulated slowly, by letter or rumor, now moved quickly through these rooms. Some historians argue that the coffee house functioned as an early public sphere: a space where opinion could form through discussion rather than being handed down by church or crown.

The authorities were uneasy. In 1675, the king issued a proclamation ordering the coffee houses closed, on the grounds that they spread "false, malicious and scandalous reports." The order provoked such immediate opposition that it was withdrawn within days, and the houses continued to operate for another century.

options.D: the architecture of seventeenth-century London

explanation: O texto traça como as coffee houses viraram centros de informação e discussão pública. (A)/(C)/(D) são detalhes ou não constam.

stimulus.title: Exercício C3: ciências sociais (meta de 6 min)
stimulus.content:
PASSAGE: The Strength of Weak Ties

When people look for a new job, common sense suggests they should turn to their closest contacts: family and good friends who know them well and want to help. Yet when the sociologist Mark Granovetter studied professionals who had recently changed jobs, he found the opposite. Of those who had found their position through a personal contact, most had heard about it not from a close friend but from an acquaintance — someone they saw only occasionally.

Granovetter's explanation rests on how information moves through social networks. Your close friends tend to know one another and move in the same circles you do, so they mostly hear the same news you already have. An acquaintance, by contrast, moves in a different circle and hears different news. A weak tie is therefore a bridge to parts of the network you could not otherwise reach.

The finding has been extended beyond job-hunting: weak ties have been linked to the spread of new ideas between organizations and to innovation within companies, where teams connected to many outside groups tend to produce more original work. Critics note that weak ties carry less trust, so acting on their information involves more risk. But the core insight has held up: the contacts most likely to tell you something new are often the ones you know least well.

options.B: weak ties often supply new information because they link us to other parts of a network
options.C: social networks have no effect on how people find jobs
options.D: Granovetter's study has been completely disproved

explanation: Tese central: weak ties frequentemente trazem informação mais nova porque conectam a outras partes da rede. (A) contradiz o achado; (C)/(D) distorcem.

stimulus.title: Exercício C4: ecologia urbana (meta de 5 min)
stimulus.content:
PASSAGE: Green Roofs in Modern Cities

Many modern cities are replacing dark, flat building roofs with "green roofs" covered in soil and low-growing plants. Unlike traditional dark roofs, which absorb sunlight and make buildings very hot, green roofs use living plants to shade the surface and cool the air through evaporation.

This simple design brings two main benefits to urban neighborhoods. First, it lowers indoor temperatures during the summer, so people inside the building use less electricity for air conditioning. Second, the layer of soil acts like a sponge during heavy rain, holding water that would otherwise flood city streets and storm drains.

However, not every building can support a green roof right away. Wet soil is heavy, so engineers must first check the strength of the roof structure. For older buildings, owners often choose thin layers of hardy succulent plants called sedums, which need very little soil or watering to survive.

options.D: Succulent plants called sedums are the only plants that can grow on city roofs.

explanation: A passagem apresenta o que são os telhados verdes, seus dois benefícios principais no calor e na chuva, e o cuidado com o peso na estrutura, o que resume a visão geral dos telhados verdes na opção (A). A alternativa (D) pega um exemplo específico do último parágrafo e o transforma em regra única.

Along the cool coast of the North Pacific, giant kelp grows from the ocean floor toward the sunlight, forming thick underwater forests. These kelp forests provide food and shelter for hundreds of marine species, including young fish, crabs, and seals.

Sea otters play a central role in keeping these forests healthy. Otters eat large numbers of sea urchins, which are small, spiny animals that crawl along the rocks and feed on the base of kelp stems. stimulus.content:
PASSAGE: Roman Concrete and Volcanic Ash

Modern steel-reinforced concrete is strong, yet harbor walls made with it often begin to crack and crumble after only a few decades in saltwater. By contrast, concrete piers and breakwaters built by Roman engineers more than two thousand years ago still stand intact along the Mediterranean coast, battered daily by waves.

For a long time, researchers knew that the Roman recipe mixed lime and volcanic rock with a powdery volcanic ash called pozzolana, taken from the region around the Bay of Naples. Only recently, however, did mineralogists discover what happens inside this mixture over time. As seawater filters through tiny pores in the concrete, it dissolves part of the volcanic ash and reacts with the lime to grow rare, interlocking crystal plates.

Instead of weakening the structure, seawater actually reinforces it: whenever a microscopic crack opens, new crystals form and seal the gap before it can spread. Material scientists are now studying this self-healing chemistry in hopes of designing modern marine concrete that lasts longer and requires fewer costly repairs.

stimulus.content:
PASSAGE: The Testing Effect in Memory Retention

When preparing for an exam, most students rely on rereading their notes or textbook chapters until the material feels familiar. Although this habit builds confidence in the short term, cognitive psychologists have repeatedly shown that passive review is one of the least effective ways to store information for the long run.

A far stronger strategy is retrieval practice, often called the "testing effect." In classic experiments, students who read a passage once and then practiced recalling its key points from memory without looking at the text scored much higher on a test a week later than students who spent the same amount of time rereading the passage four times.

Researchers explain that the act of pulling a memory out of storage alters the memory trace itself, strengthening the neural pathways connected to that knowledge. Even when a student struggles or fails to recall an answer at first, the effort makes the subsequent correction stick more firmly. Because rereading feels smooth and effortless, learners often mistake temporary fluency for lasting mastery.

stimulus.content:
PASSAGE: Subsurface Oceans on Icy Moons

For decades, astronomers searching for liquid water beyond Earth focused on the "habitable zone," the orbital band around a star where a planet's surface is warm enough for liquid water but not so hot that it boils away. By that standard, the outer solar system seemed far too cold to host liquid oceans, since sunlight at the distance of Jupiter and Saturn is a tiny fraction of what reaches Earth.

Space probe missions forced scientists to revise that view. Beneath the fractured ice crusts of moons such as Jupiter's Europa and Saturn's Enceladus lie global oceans of liquid saltwater. The heat that keeps these oceans from freezing solid does not come from the Sun, but from tidal flexing: as a moon travels along a slightly oval orbit, the immense gravitational pull of its giant planet stretches and compresses the moon's interior, generating friction and warmth.

At Enceladus, the Cassini spacecraft even flew through plumes of water vapor erupting from cracks near the south pole, detecting salts, organic molecules, and molecular hydrogen, a gas that on Earth forms around deep-sea hydrothermal vents. Such findings suggest that habitable environments may not require a warm planetary surface at all, greatly expanding the number of worlds where microbial life might arise.

options.D: Astronomers have abandoned the search for water on planets outside our solar system to focus solely on Europa.

For decades, astronomers searching for liquid water beyond Earth focused on the "habitable zone," the orbital band around a star where a planet's surface is warm enough for liquid water but not so hot that it boils away. By that standard, the outer solar system seemed far too cold to host liquid oceans, since sunlight at the distance of Jupiter and Saturn is a tiny fraction of what reaches Earth.

Such findings suggest that habitable environments may not require a warm planetary surface at all, greatly expanding the number of worlds where microbial life might arise.

stimulus.title: Exercício C9: economia e energia (meta de 6 min)
stimulus.content:
PASSAGE: The Jevons Paradox and Energy Efficiency

Intuitively, technological improvements that make machines more fuel-efficient should reduce overall fuel consumption. In 1865, however, the English economist William Stanley Jevons observed that the introduction of James Watt's far more efficient steam engine had produced the opposite result: Britain's total coal consumption soared rather than declined.

Jevons argued that efficiency lowers the effective cost of using a resource. Because Watt's engine burned much less coal per unit of work, operating steam power became profitable in industries and factories where it had previously been too expensive. As steam engines spread into textiles, mining, and railways, the surge in new uses more than offset the fuel saved by each individual machine, a rebound effect now known as the Jevons paradox.

Contemporary energy economists point out that the paradox does not occur with identical force in every sector. When demand for a service is already largely saturated, such as home refrigeration in wealthy countries, efficiency gains genuinely cut total electricity use. Where lower operating costs unlock substantial new demand, however, engineers and policymakers cannot rely on efficiency alone to curb resource depletion, and must pair technical advances with conservation policies or pricing limits.

**PASSAGE: Coral Bleaching and Thermal Stress**

Coral reefs, despite occupying less than one percent of the ocean floor, support roughly a quarter of all known marine species. This disproportionate biodiversity depends on a delicate symbiotic relationship between coral polyps and microscopic algae called zooxanthellae, which live within coral tissue and supply the majority of the coral's energy through photosynthesis. When ocean temperatures rise even slightly above a coral's tolerance threshold — often by as little as one or two degrees Celsius sustained over several weeks — the algae are expelled, leaving the coral's white calcium carbonate skeleton visible. This phenomenon, known as bleaching, does not itself kill the coral immediately, but it severs the primary energy supply, leaving the organism vulnerable to starvation and disease. Recovery is possible if temperatures normalize quickly, but repeated bleaching events, now increasingly common under sustained ocean warming, leave reefs with progressively less time to recover between episodes.

**PASSAGE 2: The Printing Press and the Standardization of Language**

Before the spread of print in fifteenth-century Europe, a single language could vary so much from region to region that speakers a few hundred kilometers apart struggled to read one another's writing. Scribes copied texts by hand, and each copy absorbed the copyist's own spelling habits and regional vocabulary.

The printing press changed the economics of this situation. A printer who set a book in type was making a substantial investment and needed to sell copies across as wide an area as possible to recover the cost. Printers therefore had a direct financial incentive to choose spelling and grammar that the largest number of readers would accept. Over several decades, the dialect of the commercially dominant region (often the capital or the largest trading city) tended to become the basis of the printed standard, not because it was linguistically superior, but because it reached the biggest market.

This standardizing effect was not entirely welcome. Writers who spoke regional varieties found their own usage increasingly marked as incorrect, and forms of the language that were never printed came to be seen as mere "dialect" rather than legitimate versions of the language. Many historians now argue that the "standard" form of many European languages owes less to any natural center of the language than to which city happened to dominate early printing.

stimulus.content:
**PASSAGE: The Economics of Network Effects**

A network effect occurs when a product or service becomes more valuable as more people use it. The telephone is the textbook example: a single telephone is useless, but each new user adds value for everyone already connected. Such effects can be direct or indirect. Direct network effects arise among users of the *same* product: a messaging app is more useful as more of one's contacts join it. Indirect network effects arise between two distinct but interdependent groups: a ride-sharing platform becomes more attractive to riders as more drivers join, and more attractive to drivers as more riders join.

Because users generally prefer the platform with the largest existing network, early leaders in such markets tend to compound their advantage rapidly, often keeping dominant positions even when competitors offer superior technology. This "winner-take-most" dynamic has generated significant regulatory concern, particularly about whether dominant platforms use their market power in ways that stifle competition rather than simply reflecting superior efficiency.

Critics of this narrative, however, caution against treating network effects as an insurmountable barrier to entry. Several dominant platforms have been displaced by newer entrants offering a sufficiently different experience. Low switching costs, multi-homing behavior (where users maintain accounts on multiple competing platforms at once), and shifts in user preference can erode even substantial network advantages over time.

The telephone is the textbook example: a single telephone is useless, but each new user adds value for everyone already connected. Such effects can be direct or indirect. Direct network effects arise among users of the *same* product: a messaging app is more useful as more of one's contacts join it. Indirect network effects arise between two distinct but interdependent groups: a ride-sharing platform becomes more attractive to riders as more drivers join, and more attractive to drivers as more riders join.

Because users generally prefer the platform with the largest existing network, early leaders in such markets tend to compound their advantage rapidly, often keeping dominant positions even when competitors offer superior technology. This "winner-take-most" dynamic has generated significant regulatory concern, particularly about whether dominant platforms use their market power in ways that stifle competition rather than simply reflecting superior efficiency.

Critics of this narrative, however, caution against treating network effects as an insurmountable barrier to entry. Several dominant platforms have been displaced by newer entrants offering a sufficiently different experience. Low switching costs, multi-homing behavior (where users maintain accounts on multiple competing platforms at once), and shifts in user preference can erode even substantial network advantages over time.
